name: Umar Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the buying team at Kestrel Building Supply, which stocks timber, plumbing fittings and insulation for trade counters across three small towns. My mornings are price lists: checking what the sawmills and pipe makers are charging this week and deciding how much to lock in. Afternoons I'm on calls with suppliers or down at the yard, looking at a bowed batch of joists someone wants to send back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the parts that wear you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being good at the job and still counting coins. Kestrel pays less than the big chains, but they're two hours away, so I stay. My partner Rosa is a teaching assistant, I send my younger brother something for his college fees each month, and we've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the chatbot stays a chatbot. Fine by me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools are handy for the boring bits and leave it there. I use one now and then to tidy a supplier email or pull prices out of a messy PDF. Online I'd probably share a joke about all the money investors burned on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is safe, but safe at a wage that barely covers us. Timber prices jump every spring and the builders pay us late, so Kestrel is always nervous about cash. A plateau doesn't touch any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, but I'd use the bit of time the tools save to get our supplier contracts in order, because that's what gets you a raise at review. I'd ask the staff association to push for pay closer to the city rate. And I'd stop sending my brother money for a few months, if he can manage, to rebuild a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with that background hum about money. Nothing frightening. Just the same tightness at the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your brother's fees. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. My brother Tariq would say it's fine, and then I'd find out he skipped meals. I'd probably cut it in half rather than stop it, and make it up to him later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push harder for a raise if AI wasn't a threat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because then I know Kestrel needs me. Right now the owners hint that software might do my job, and it makes everyone quiet at review time. If AI went away as a threat, I'd ask for what I'm worth at review time.

say: I'd say AI tools are **handy for boring bits**, like tidying supplier emails.
I'd joke online about the **money investors burned** chasing it.
think: My job is **safe**, but at a wage that barely covers us.
Spring **timber prices** and late-paying builders keep Kestrel nervous about cash.
do: Use saved time to tidy **supplier contracts** before his annual review.
Ask the staff association to push for **city-rate pay**.
Halve the money he sends his **brother** to rebuild savings.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **background hum** about money at month's end.
S0.quote: If AI went away as a threat, I'd ask for what I'm worth at review time.
fieldNote: He uses AI **now and then** and sees it as a helper, not a rival, in this picture.
The plateau would make him **bolder about pay**, since the threat of software keeps staff quiet.
Money strain comes from **family support** and low local pay, not from AI.

steps.text: Tidy Kestrel's supplier contracts before his annual review
Ask the staff association to seek city-rate pay
Halve monthly money to Tariq for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying's on that list. And planning, and checking. That's most of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this has to be done with staff, not to us. I'd want the firm to tell us which tasks are moving and what happens to the people doing them. I'd share stories online of firms that retrained their buyers instead of sacking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team of three becomes me and a system. The juniors, Lena and Kofi, would go first, and I'd be the one asked to train the tool on their work. That would sit badly with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the ordering software properly, once a couple of other merchants had shown it works, because being the person who runs it keeps me employed. I'd go to the staff association and ask for a written plan for Lena and Kofi, like moving them to the trade counter. And Rosa and I would cancel the trip to her parents' this summer to save around six hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Torn. Relieved it might not be me, guilty that it might be them. And still worried, because one owner's mood could change all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train the tool on their work. Would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think I'd refuse. If I refuse to train the ordering software, they bring in a consultant and I'm out as well. I'd do it and fight for my juniors at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena and Kofi when the news came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my two juniors the truth over lunch at the cafe by the yard, not in a meeting room. Then I'd help them write CVs that night. Kofi's got a baby on the way, which makes it worse.

say: I'd say change must be done **with staff**, not to us.
I'd ask the firm to say **which tasks move** and what happens to the people.
think: My team of three shrinks to **me and a system**.
My juniors would go first, and I'd be asked to **train the tool** on their work.
do: Learn the **ordering software** once other merchants show it works.
Ask the staff association for a **written plan** for his juniors.
Cancel the summer trip to **save about six hundred**.
feel: **Relieved** for himself and **guilty** about his juniors at once.
Still worried, because one **owner's mood** could change everything.
S1.quote: If I refuse to train the ordering software, they bring in a consultant and I'm out as well. I'd do it and fight for my juniors at the same time.
fieldNote: He moves **once it's proven**, waiting for other merchants before committing to the tool.
He feels **responsible for juniors** Lena and Kofi and wants a plan for them.
His job looks **survivable** but not secure, so he keeps planning and saving.

steps.text: Learn Kestrel's ordering software after two merchants prove it
Ask the staff association for a plan for Lena and Kofi
Cancel the summer trip to Rosa's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd barely have learned the new system before it learned me out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a public safety net now, not after the damage. I'd back the unions and anyone calling for a tax on AI profits. At work I'd tell people to keep records of everything, in case there's a payout fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone by 2028. Buying is pure thinking work and AGI does it better and cheaper. The yard work, unloading and checking timber, might last until robots arrive around 2031, but that pays even less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move on it fast. In the first three months I'd sign up for an evening course in site logistics, the job of getting materials onto building sites on time, because it's half on your feet. I'd ask Kestrel's yard foreman about weekend shifts to bring in extra. And Rosa and I would give up the flat and move in with her parents to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed. I could cope with change, but not with change that outruns me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Rosa's parents. How would that land at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa would be fine with it. I'd be the one struggling, a thirty-year-old in a box room. But it saves eight hundred a month, and that buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your brother's fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to stop them. I'd tell Tariq straight, and probably cry about it afterwards in the car. He'd need to find a loan or a part-time job.

say: I'd say we need a **public safety net** now, before the damage.
I'd back calls for a **tax on AI profits** and tell colleagues to keep records.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028** because it's pure thinking work.
Yard work lasts until **robots around 2031**, but it pays even less.
do: Start an evening **site logistics** course within three months.
Ask the yard foreman for **weekend shifts**.
Give up the flat and move in with **Rosa's parents**.
feel: **Alarmed** by the speed of change outrunning him.
S2.quote: I could cope with change, but not with change that outruns me.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** sensibly, moving toward half-hands-on site logistics work.
Ending his **brother's support** is the hardest cut for him.
His public line is **political**, a tax on AI profits, while privately he plans to move fast.

steps.text: Start an evening course in site logistics within three months
Ask Kestrel's yard foreman for weekend shifts
Give up the flat and move in with Rosa's parents
Back campaigns for a tax on AI profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do something. Not enough to do it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the window for governments to set up retraining and income support, and I'd tell people to vote on it. At work I'd say let's plan this together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine for maybe three of the five years, because I'd be the person running the buying system. After 2031 the buying goes, and I'd need to be somewhere else already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd learn the ordering AI properly, because it makes me useful now. In year two, I'd start the site logistics course at night. I'd also try to save five hundred a month once Tariq finishes college, so we've got a few months behind us when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not frozen. I can see a path. It's just narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn the AI if it's going to take the job anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it pays the bills in the meantime and it shows me how these things think. If I'm going into site logistics, I'll be working alongside them there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your union or association in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deal: notice of at least a year, and the firm pays for one course per person. That's not radical. Kestrel could afford it from what it saves on salaries.

say: I'd say these **five years** are the window for retraining and income support.
I'd tell people to **vote on it** and ask colleagues to plan together.
think: I'd be fine for **about three years** while I run the system.
After 2031 buying goes, so I need to **be elsewhere** already.
do: Learn the **ordering AI** properly in the first year.
Start a **site logistics** course at night in year two.
Save **five hundred a month** once his brother finishes college.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, seeing a **narrow path** ahead.
S3.quote: I'd be fine for maybe three of the five years, because I'd be the person running the buying system.
fieldNote: He uses AI as a **bridge**: it pays now and teaches him for the next job.
His **union ask** is modest and costed, typical of his steady style.
His savings plan hinges on his **brother finishing college**.

steps.text: Learn Kestrel's ordering AI properly in the first year
Start a night course in site logistics in year two
Save five hundred a month after Tariq graduates
Ask the association for a year's notice and paid courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade's long enough that I'd be a different person by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this fairly, so no excuses. I'd want public courses, strong rules on layoffs, and buyers given first chance at the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years would make me relax too much. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with a kid, and suddenly my whole trade is software. The time would help only if I used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more at work over the next couple of years, then move into site logistics around year four. I'd keep up with the association and try to build three months of savings by thirty. Rosa and I might wait a couple of years for a child until I'm in the new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier, but not calm. I'd still have the buying job dying, just slower. And robots coming three years later means the site work isn't forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned waiting on a child. Is that new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about it for after thirty. With ten years' warning I'd want to switch careers first, so the baby doesn't arrive while I'm on a trainee wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually use the time instead of relaxing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline from outside. If Kestrel said buying ends in 2033, I'd be enrolled the next week. Vague warnings don't move me.

say: I'd say we've got **time** to do this fairly, so there are no excuses.
I'd want public courses, **layoff rules** and buyers first in line for new jobs.
think: Ten years would make me **relax too much** and put off the switch.
At thirty-seven, maybe with a child, my **whole trade** could be software.
do: Use **AI at work** more over the next two years.
Move into **site logistics** around year four.
Build **three months** of savings by age thirty.
feel: **Steadier** but not calm, knowing site work faces **robots** later too.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd want to switch careers first, so the baby doesn't arrive while I'm on a trainee wage.
fieldNote: Time helps him only with an **outside deadline**; vague warnings don't move him.
A **child** would be delayed until after the career switch.
He tracks the **robot lag**, knowing site logistics only buys him a few more years.

steps.text: Use AI tools more in Kestrel's buying over two years
Move into site logistics around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for a steady person like me. What would help is notice from my employer, a paid course, and some public income for the months in between.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who they'd worry about at work. I'd worry about Kofi and Lena before myself, and I think lots of team leads feel like that.

headlineQuote: Being good at the job and still counting coins.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old team lead** buying timber and fittings at Kestrel Building Supply, on low pay.
He and Rosa have **two weeks' savings**, and he helps pay his brother's college fees.
He uses AI **now and then** and would learn the ordering tool once it's proven.
He fears for his **juniors** in Steady Disruption and expects to lose buying by AGI.
His plan is **site logistics**, a half-hands-on job, backed by union and political pressure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a steady person like him has no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** from employers, a **paid course** and public income for the gap months.
